One box-kite as an octahedron

Six assessors on ±x, ±y, ±z; the edges are the products that vanish. Click a vertex. A picture shows a structure; it is not evidence that the structure means anything beyond its definition.

← Box-kite gallery

orbit: off
About this visual

What you are looking at. One box-kite: six assessors joined by the products that vanish. An assessor (a, b) is the plane spanned by e_a and e_(b+8) in the sedenions, drawn here as the label (a, b+8). Its two diagonals e_a ± e_(b+8) are zero-divisors: multiplied by the right diagonal of another assessor they give exactly zero. Each vertex is one assessor, each edge is a pair of assessors whose diagonals annihilate each other. The six vertices sit on ±x, ±y, ±z, so the shape is an octahedron, K2,2,2.

How to read it. Choose the strut s (the XOR of a and b, the same for all six). Drag to turn the octahedron; click a vertex. Its four neighbours light up and the panel lists, for each of its two diagonals, the four diagonals it annihilates, found by multiplying out in the browser. The three dashed lines through the centre are the reversal pairs (a, b) and (b, a): the only pairs in the kite that do NOT annihilate each other. The coloured gizmo in the corner names the axes by the pair they carry.

What it shows. Every vertex has exactly four neighbours and one non-neighbour, the reversal partner. The Laplacian spectrum of the graph (switch it on) is {0, 4, 4, 4, 6, 6} for every strut: one zero mode, a triple mode at 4, a double at 6. All seven struts give the same picture, only the labels change.

What it does not show. That the octahedron is a place in space. The six axes are drawn at right angles because the graph is K2,2,2; the zero-divisors themselves live in 16 dimensions. e0 is not in the picture on purpose: it is outside every box-kite. The frame has no σ = ½ marker because it has no σ coordinate; the only balance in it is the equal split of each diagonal into 1/√2 and ±1/√2.

Numbers to check. 6 vertices, 12 edges, 3 non-edges (the reversal pairs), 4-regular; spectrum [0,4,4,4,6,6]; each diagonal annihilates 4 others (84 diagonals × 4 = 336 ordered pairs). Strut 1 is de Marrais's Box-Kite I: (3,10) (2,11) (5,12) (4,13) (7,14) (6,15) in his notation.

running self-check…

Code and data. Everything shown is recomputed in the browser by bk.js (the Cayley–Dickson table by doubling, every product, the group by enumeration) and compared with the numbers the Python engine baked into bk_data.js.

  • ValaQuenta/modules/box_kite/maths.py: the Python engine these pages port and check against (Cayley–Dickson table, assessors, box-kites, associator, the labelled group)
  • ValaQuenta/wiki/box_kite.md: the engine's record page, including 'The group, enumerated'
  • Ainulindale/wiki/84_the_box_kite_debugger.md: the narrative of the box-kite as a debugger
  • ValaQuenta/tests/test_box_kite.py: the tests, including an independent recursive Cayley–Dickson product

Literature.

  • R. P. C. de Marrais, "The 42 Assessors and the Box-Kites They Fly: Diagonal Axis-Pair Systems of Zero-Divisors in the Sedenions' 16 Dimensions", arXiv:math/0011260 (2000).
  • R. P. C. de Marrais, "Placeholder Substructures I: The Road from Zero-Divisors to the 84 Diagonal Sedenions" and "II: The Emergence of the Pentagonal Genes", arXiv:math/0207003 and arXiv:math/0207005.
  • K. Imaeda and M. Imaeda, "Sedenions: algebra and analysis", Applied Mathematics and Computation 115 (2000) 77–88.
  • R. E. Cawagas, "On the structure and zero divisors of the Cayley–Dickson sedenion algebra", Discussiones Mathematicae – General Algebra and Applications 24 (2004) 251–265.
  • J. C. Baez, "The Octonions", Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 39 (2002) 145–205. The octonions, the Fano plane, the automorphism group G₂, the 480 multiplication tables.
  • J. H. Conway and D. A. Smith, On Quaternions and Octonions (A K Peters, 2003). The 1344 and the 168 in the labelled octonion group.
  • J. H. Conway, R. T. Curtis, S. P. Norton, R. A. Parker, R. A. Wilson, Atlas of Finite Groups (Oxford, 1985): L₃(2) = PSL(2,7), order 168.
  • The Python Software Foundation, Python 3 documentation: itertools.permutations, itertools.product.
  • OpenSCAD User Manual (camera, projection, text, polyhedron).
  • MDN Web Docs, Canvas API.
